The African rock python (Python sebae) exhibits a substantial size at hatching, with neonates emerging from their parchment-shelled eggs measuring approximately 40 cm [Lb = approximately 40 cm] in total length after a developmental period that hinges critically on thermal conditions. When eggs are incubated at a steady 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the age at birth is documented at 82 days [ab = 82 days], a duration that aligns closely with the reported range of 65 to 80 days observed in controlled captive settings for this species. This incubation period is relatively extended compared to smaller pythonids, reflecting the large yolk volume invested in each leathery-shelled egg. The transition from an incubating egg to a free-living hatchling marks a significant physiological shift, as the young snake must commence exogenous feeding shortly after absorbing its remaining yolk reserves. At emergence, the hatchling is already an independent juvenile, capable of subduing small prey items despite its modest dimensions, which typically fall within a range of 35 to 45 cm in total length.

By the time they reach adulthood, African rock pythons achieve formidable dimensions, with an ultimate total length recorded at 550 cm [Li = 550 cm] in some of the largest verified specimens, surpassing the maximum of 480 cm sometimes cited in earlier literature. This extraordinary size places Python sebae among the most massive snake species globally, comparable only to the reticulated python and the green anaconda. Corresponding to this impressive length, the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown individual can reach approximately 89,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 89,000 grams], a figure derived from length-weight relationships observed in closely related large-bodied pythons. This enormous body mass is supported by a generalist diet that includes medium-to-large mammals and birds, allowing the snakes to accumulate substantial fat reserves that sustain them through periods of fasting. The attainment of such a large terminal size requires many years of consistent feeding and favorable environmental conditions, as growth rates decelerate markedly once the snake approaches its asymptotic dimensions. Field data suggest that females typically grow larger than males in this species.

Neonatal mass is surprisingly modest given the potential adult size, as hatchling African rock pythons weigh approximately 161 grams [Wwb = approximately 161 grams] at emergence. This birth weight, which scales allometrically with the cube of the length ratio between neonates and mature adults, represents a substantial investment per offspring but is consistent with the production of relatively few, large eggs typical of boid snakes. The yolk-laden egg from which the hatchling emerges contains all the nutrients required to sustain the snake through its first weeks of life until it locates its first prey. After absorbing its endogenous yolk stores, the young juvenile must quickly develop its hunting skills, typically feeding on small rodents and lizards. This initial body mass is a critical determinant of early survival, as larger hatchlings enjoy a reduced risk of predation and can subdue a broader range of prey items. The transition from yolk dependence to active feeding represents a high-mortality period in the species' life history.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 27 °C [T = 27 °C], female African rock pythons attain reproductive maturity at approximately four years [tR = approximately four years], at which point they begin producing their first egg clutches. This age at first reproduction represents a significant delay relative to many smaller snake species, a consequence of the prolonged growth phase required to reach the substantial body size necessary for successful reproduction. A mature female can produce clutches ranging from 20 to 50 eggs, and under optimal thermal conditions she may produce a single clutch each year, yielding a maximum annual reproductive rate of 20 to 50 eggs per year [Ri = 20 to 50 eggs per year], modest compared to oviparous lizards but typical for a large-bodied ambush predator. The timing of reproduction is closely linked to the seasonal availability of prey, ensuring that hatchlings emerge during periods of high small-mammal abundance. This reproductive strategy, characterized by delayed maturity and relatively low fecundity, is consistent with a slow life-history pace.

The maximum lifespan of the African rock python, documented in both wild populations and captive individuals maintained at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], has been recorded at over 30 years [am = over 30 years], with some captive specimens living well beyond 12 years, the figure often cited in general references. This remarkable longevity, among the highest recorded for any snake species, reflects a life-history strategy centered on low adult mortality and sustained reproductive output over many decades. As a reproductively active adult, a female may continue producing clutches annually for much of her adult life, with reproductive senescence appearing only in the oldest individuals. The gradual accumulation of somatic damage and the eventual breakdown of physiological homeostasis ultimately lead to natural mortality, though predation by large mammals, crocodiles, and human activity likely truncates lifespan in many wild populations. The species' slow growth, delayed maturity, and extended reproductive window together shape a demographic profile typical of a top predator occupying a stable ecological niche.
